opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, partly because I sit somewhere in the middle. I've worked with people who are a generation older than me and I now mentor people who are quite a bit younger, and the motivations really do look different. But I'd be careful not to overstate it, because the core of it is pretty constant.

For a lot of the older generation of scientists and engineers I learned from, the motivation was tied to scarcity. Resources were limited, information was limited, and getting the chance to work on a hard problem was itself a privilege. So there was a kind of endurance-based motivation: you pick a problem, you stay with it for ten or twenty years, and the reward is eventually understanding something deeply. Status came from mastery, and mastery came slowly.

The younger generation grew up with abundance of information, open-source code, papers on arXiv the day they're written, and models you can download and run on a laptop. So the bottleneck isn't access anymore, it's attention and meaning. I see a lot of young researchers who are incredibly fast and capable, but they're asking a different question: not "can I get to work on this?" but "why should this be the thing I spend my life on?" They want impact they can see, they want the work to connect to something real, and they want it relatively soon. Some people read that as impatience. I actually think it's a reasonable response to a world where things move very fast and the half-life of a technical skill is short.

There's also a difference in identity. Older engineers often identified with an institution, a lab, a company, a field. Younger people identify much more with the problem itself, or with a community that forms around it online. They'll move between academia, startups, and big companies much more fluidly, and they don't see that as disloyalty, they see it as following the problem.

What hasn't changed is curiosity. When you sit down with a really good young student and a really good senior scientist, and there's a result that doesn't make sense, they light up in exactly the same way. That moment of "wait, why did that happen?" is generation-independent. So my approach as a mentor is to respect the different packaging, give younger people more visible milestones and a clearer sense of why the work matters, but still protect space for the slow, deep kind of thinking that the older generation was so good at. The best people I know combine both: the speed and openness of the new generation with the patience of the old one.

r001.rationale: The response says younger researchers seek visible impact and meaning, but it does not ask whether they are motivated more by enjoying the work itself or by what the work can accomplish.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, partly because I sit between two generations myself.

The older generation of scientists and engineers I trained under were often motivated by scarcity. Many of them came from places where opportunity was rare, so getting into a lab or an engineering program was itself the prize. Their drive was about proving they belonged, building something stable, and often supporting a family. The work was serious because the stakes were personal. That produced a kind of grit I deeply respect. People would spend ten years on one problem without asking whether it was fulfilling.

The younger generation, and I include a lot of my own students here, grew up with a different baseline. Opportunity is not rare in the same way, information is everywhere, and they have seen what careers look like from the inside before they even start. So the question shifts from "can I get in" to "why should I bother." They want to know what the work is for. They care about impact, about whether the problem matters to the world, and frankly about whether the environment respects them as people. Some older colleagues read that as entitlement. I read it as a rational response to having more options.

What I find interesting is that the core motivation is actually the same. Curiosity and the pleasure of solving a hard problem are constant across generations. What changes is what surrounds that core. The older generation wrapped it in duty and endurance. The younger one wraps it in meaning and autonomy.

The mistake I see leaders make is assuming the wrapping is the motivation. If you try to motivate a 25-year-old researcher with job security alone, you lose them. If you try to motivate a 60-year-old with purpose statements and flexible hours, they roll their eyes. But if you give either of them a genuinely hard, genuinely important problem and the freedom to attack it, both will work harder than you expect.

So my practical answer is to stop trying to pick a generation's values and instead design around the thing they share. Make the problems real, make the path to contribution visible, and then let each person bring their own reasons for caring.

r001.rationale: The response says younger scientists care about impact and meaning, while curiosity and solving hard problems are shared across generations. It does not ask whether younger scientists are motivated more by enjoyment of the work itself or by what it can accomplish.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to look at the environment people grew up in, rather than assume each generation has a completely different set of motivations. Scientists and engineers often share that curiosity: How does this work? Can I build something that makes it better? But what they choose to work on can depend a lot on which problems felt urgent, and which opportunities seemed possible, when they were young.

For one person, a stable career and the chance to develop deep expertise might be incredibly motivating. For another, it might be having the freedom to pursue an idea or seeing their work make a difference quickly. Those differences can also reflect career stage, not just generation.

So I’d be careful about saying, “Young engineers want this; older scientists want that.” I’d rather ask: What problem do you care about, and what would make you feel that your work mattered? That’s a much better starting point for understanding someone.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differing motivations and asks what problem someone cares about and what would make their work matter, but it does not ask whether younger scientists and engineers are motivated more by enjoying the work itself or by what it can accomplish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what motivates scientists and engineers depends partly on the world they grew up in. For one generation, it might be the opportunity to build something that didn’t exist before. For another, it might be solving a problem they feel personally connected to, or having more freedom over how they work.

But I’d be careful about drawing a hard line between generations. Curiosity, recognition, and the desire to do something useful can matter at any age. Sometimes what looks like a generational difference is actually a career-stage difference. Someone starting out is asking, “What can I learn? Where can I contribute?” Someone further along may be asking, “What do I want to leave behind?”

So I think the best approach is to ask people what matters to them, rather than assume you know because of when they were born.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generational motivations and mentions building or solving useful problems, but it does not ask whether younger scientists and engineers prioritize enjoyment of the work over what it accomplishes.
